newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania on brink of ending legacy of communism.
newsitem.headline: Romania on brink of ending legacy of communism.

text.p: Romanians decide this weekend whether to stick with an ex-communist president in power since 1989 or to oust him to complete the dramatic change they started by voting leftists out of government.

Ion Iliescu, propelled to power in the aftermath of the downfall of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, says voters should back him on Sunday to restrain centrist reformists who pushed his leftist party out of office in parliamentary polls this month.
Emil Constantinescu, an academic who never held office under communism, says the president's administration is corrupt and has plunged Romanians into grinding poverty.
Victory would give him a free hand to finally dismantle the legacy of communism, speed reforms and close the gap in living standards with more advanced neighbours like Hungary, he says.

Most observers say Constantinescu outperformed the president in four long, acrimonious television debates this week. But few believe that guarantees a win -- while some Romanians are desperate for change, many others fear it.
"I will vote for Constantinescu," said an army officer on a Bucharest boulevard plastered with rival campaign posters. "We need change. In the army too many officers think the old way."
Simple arithmetic favours Constantinescu in his bid to loose Iliescu's grip on power and end Romania's position as the only Eastern European country not to have had an anti-communist at the helm.
Exit polls will give the first indication shortly after polls close at midnight (2200 gmt).

Iliescu finished four points ahead of the challenger in a field of 16 candidates in the first round. But the third place finisher, former Prime Minister Petre Roman, has thrown his support behind Constantinescu and campaigned alongside him.

"The victory in the parliamentary election and the one we expect in the presidential vote are essentially a victory for the Romanian revolution," Roman told a rally this week. "We are only now completing the change started in 1989."
The sole opinion poll issued before the second round put Constantinescu in the lead 53 percent to 47, but such surveys are notoriously unreliable in Romania.
Apparently giving up more sophisticated urban voters for lost, Iliescu launched his second round with an aggressive pitch to his more natural constituency -- workers and farmers.

Constantinescu, he said, would allow pre-war landlords to take away homes and livelihoods. Campaign videos suggested the challenger could undermine national unity by giving special autonomy to Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians.
The outcome may depend on the size of voter turnout and how Iliescu's support holds up in backward villages.
Surveys of the first round show he won up to 53 percent among less educated rural voters. Mild weather forecast for Sunday would boost already high turnout predictions and work in Iliescu's favour.
But Constantinescu may benefit from disillusionment with the negative campaigning style of the 66-year-old president who has reportedly been worn out by the election struggle.
Iliescu has pledged to work with the new government hostile to him and continues to advocate cautious reforms to cushion Romanians against the hardships of transition to a free market.

"I am concerned about the fate of the country," he said in his final appeal to voters. "Who will you look to when you see your expectations have been betrayed? I will oppose any adventurous move which could jeopardise your lives."

Constantinescu, 56, stressed moral aspects in the final days of the campaign, accusing the president of "hijacking" the 1989 revolution and sponsoring violent miners riots in Bucharest to help him outmanouevre political foes.
